claim: The Drosophila mushroom body (MB) is an associative center in invertebrate brains.
source: We identified the neurons comprising the Drosophila mushroom body (MB), an associative center in invertebrate brains, and provide a comprehensive map describing their potential connections.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work establishing the MB's role in learning and memory.

claim: Each of the 21 MB output neuron (MBON) types elaborates segregated dendritic arbors along the parallel axons of ∼2000 Kenyon cells.
source: Each of the 21 MB output neuron (MBON) types elaborates segregated dendritic arbors along the parallel axons of ∼2000 Kenyon cells, forming 15 compartments that collectively tile the MB lobes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the anatomical data presented in the manuscript, including confocal imaging, computational alignment, and split-GAL4 driver lines that visualize individual MBON types.

claim: MBON dendritic arbors form 15 compartments that collectively tile the MB lobes.
source: Each of the 21 MB output neuron (MBON) types elaborates segregated dendritic arbors along the parallel axons of ∼2000 Kenyon cells, forming 15 compartments that collectively tile the MB lobes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational alignment of MBON dendritic arbors and two-color labeling experiments showing segregation and tiling (Figure 10, Figure 11).

claim: MBON axons project to five discrete neuropils outside of the MB.
source: MBON axons project to five discrete neuropils outside of the MB and three MBON types form a feedforward network in the lobes.
evidence: This is supported by computational alignment of MBON axon terminals and quantification of their distribution across brain regions (Figure 18, Figure 19).

claim: Three MBON types form a feedforward network in the lobes.
source: MBON axons project to five discrete neuropils outside of the MB and three MBON types form a feedforward network in the lobes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical tracing showing that MBON-γ4>γ1γ2, MBON-β1>α, and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β project axons back into the MB lobes (Figure 17).

claim: Each of the 20 dopaminergic neuron (DAN) types projects axons to one, or at most two, of the MBON compartments.
source: Each of the 20 dopaminergic neuron (DAN) types projects axons to one, or at most two, of the MBON compartments.
evidence: This is shown through split-GAL4 driver lines, photoactivation experiments, and computational alignment demonstrating the compartmentalized projection patterns of DANs (Figure 10, Figure 12, Figures 14-16).

claim: Convergence of DAN axons on compartmentalized Kenyon cell–MBON synapses creates a highly ordered unit that can support learning to impose valence on sensory representations.
source: Convergence of DAN axons on compartmentalized Kenyon cell–MBON synapses creates a highly ordered unit that can support learning to impose valence on sensory representations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed (compartmentalization, overlap of DAN and MBON processes) and prior functional studies cited in the manuscript showing DANs convey reward/punishment signals.

claim: Innate behaviors are mediated by genetically determined neural circuits.
source: Innate behaviors are observed in naïve animals without prior learning or experience, suggesting that they are mediated by genetically determined neural circuits.
evidence: This is a general principle in neuroscience supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Most sensory cues acquire behavioral relevance through learning.
source: Responses to most sensory stimuli, however, are not innate but experience-dependent, allowing an organism to respond appropriately in a variable and uncertain world. Thus, most sensory cues acquire behavioral relevance through learning.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in neuroscience and behavioral biology.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, a number of different forms of learning have been observed in response to sensory stimuli.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, a number of different forms of learning have been observed in response to sensory stimuli (Siegel and Hall, 1979; Liu et al., 1999, 2006; Masek and Scott, 2010; Schnaitmann et al., 2010; Ofstad et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies demonstrating various forms of learning in Drosophila.

claim: In associative olfactory learning, exposure to an odor (conditioned stimulus, CS) in association with an unconditioned stimulus (US) results in appetitive or aversive memory.
source: In associative olfactory learning, exposure to an odor (conditioned stimulus, CS) in association with an unconditioned stimulus (US) results in appetitive or aversive memory (Quinn et al., 1974; Tempel et al., 1983; Tully and Quinn, 1985).
evidence: This is a well-established principle of classical conditioning in Drosophila, supported by the cited studies.

claim: Olfactory memory formation and retrieval in insects require the mushroom body (MB).
source: Olfactory memory formation and retrieval in insects require the mushroom body (MB) (Heisenberg et al., 1985; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994, Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001), an associative center in the protocerebrum (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies demonstrating the necessity of the MB for olfactory learning and memory.

claim: The 51 glomeruli of the antennal lobe extend projection neurons (PN) to the calyx of the MB and the lateral horn (LH).
source: The 51 glomeruli of the AL extend projection neurons (PN) to the calyx of the MB and the lateral horn (LH).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: There are a total of ∼200 projection neurons in the antennal lobe.
source: There are a total of ∼200 PN; 6 from the DL3 glomerulus are shown.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: Olfactory receptor neurons expressing the same odorant receptor converge onto a single glomerulus in the antennal lobe.
source: Olfactory receptor neurons expressing the same odorant receptor converge onto a single glomerulus in the AL.
evidence: This is a well-established principle of olfactory system organization, supported by prior studies and general knowledge.

claim: A small number (generally 3–4) of PNs from each of the 51 AL glomeruli innervate the MB calyx.
source: A small number (generally 3–4) of PNs from each of the 51 AL glomeruli innervate the MB calyx where they synapse on the dendrites of the ∼2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) in a globular structure, the calyx.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is based on established knowledge of MB anatomy.

claim: Each Kenyon cell exhibits, on average, 6.4 dendritic 'claws'.
source: Each KC exhibits, on average, 6.4 dendritic 'claws' (Butcher et al., 2012), and each claw is innervated by a single PN.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Butcher et al., 2012.

claim: Each dendritic claw of a Kenyon cell is innervated by a single projection neuron.
source: Each KC exhibits, on average, 6.4 dendritic 'claws' (Butcher et al., 2012), and each claw is innervated by a single PN.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is based on established knowledge.

claim: There is little order in connection patterns of PNs to KCs.
source: There is little order in connection patterns of PNs to KCs.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is supported by citations to studies demonstrating random connectivity.

claim: KCs can be categorized into three major classes α/β, α′/β′, and γ based on their projection patterns in the lobes.
source: KCs can be categorized into three major classes α/β, α′/β′, and γ based on their projection patterns in the lobes (Crittenden et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a well-established classification supported by the cited study and general knowledge of MB anatomy.

claim: The β, β′, and γ lobes constitute the medial lobes (also known as horizontal lobes).
source: The β, β′, and γ lobes constitute the medial lobes (also known as horizontal lobes), while the α and α′ lobes constitute the vertical lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is based on established anatomical nomenclature.

claim: The α and α′ lobes constitute the vertical lobes.
source: The β, β′, and γ lobes constitute the medial lobes (also known as horizontal lobes), while the α and α′ lobes constitute the vertical lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is based on established anatomical nomenclature.

claim: The MB lobes are separately wrapped by ensheathing glia.
source: These lobes are separately wrapped by ensheathing glia (Awasaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Awasaki et al., 2008.

claim: The α/β and α′/β′ neurons bifurcate at the anterior end of the pedunculus and project to both the medial and vertical lobes.
source: The α/β and α′/β′ neurons bifurcate at the anterior end of the pedunculus and project to both the medial and vertical lobes (Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 1999 and is a well-known feature of MB anatomy.

claim: The γ neurons project only to the medial lobe.
source: The γ neurons project only to the medial lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is based on established knowledge of MB anatomy.

claim: Dendrites of MBONs and terminals of modulatory dopaminergic neurons (DANs) intersect the longitudinal axis of the KC axon bundle, forming 15 subdomains.
source: Dendrites of MBONs and terminals of modulatory dopaminergic neurons (DANs) intersect the longitudinal axis of the KC axon bundle, forming 15 subdomains, five each in the α/β, α′/β′, and γ lobes (numbered α1, α2, and α3 for subdomains in the α lobe from proximal to distal) (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2008 and is further elaborated upon with new data in this manuscript.

claim: One MBON and one DAN innervate the core of the distal pedunculus intersecting the α/β KCs.
source: Additionally, one MBON and one DAN innervate the core of the distal pedunculus intersecting the α/β KCs (pedc, see below).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and is supported by data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: There are seven types of KCs.
source: There are seven types of KCs; five of the seven types have their dendrites in the main calyx, while those of the γd cells form the vAC (Aso et al., 2009; Butcher et al., 2012) and those of the α/βp cells the dAC (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, supported by split-GAL4 driver lines and single-cell analysis.

claim: Five of the seven KC types have their dendrites in the main calyx.
source: There are seven types of KCs; five of the seven types have their dendrites in the main calyx, while those of the γd cells form the vAC (Aso et al., 2009; Butcher et al., 2012) and those of the α/βp cells the dAC (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, supported by split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical analysis.

claim: The dendrites of γd cells form the ventral accessory calyx (vAC).
source: There are seven types of KCs; five of the seven types have their dendrites in the main calyx, while those of the γd cells form the vAC (Aso et al., 2009; Butcher et al., 2012) and those of the α/βp cells the dAC (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2009 and Butcher et al., 2012.

claim: The dendrites of α/βp cells form the dorsal accessory calyx (dAC).
source: There are seven types of KCs; five of the seven types have their dendrites in the main calyx, while those of the γd cells form the vAC (Aso et al., 2009; Butcher et al., 2012) and those of the α/βp cells the dAC (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2008.

claim: The accessory calyces are thought to receive non-olfactory input since they do not receive input from the PNs from the AL.
source: The accessory calyces are thought to receive non-olfactory input since they do not receive input from the PNs from the AL (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of PN input, supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2008.

claim: Different KCs occupy distinct layers in the lobes.
source: Different KCs occupy distinct layers in the lobes as indicated (p: posterior; c: core; s: surface; m: medial; a: anterior; and d: dorsal).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrated through split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical analysis (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: Some MB extrinsic neurons extend processes to only a specific layer within a subdomain, defining elemental subdivisions in the lobes, or 'synaptic units'.
source: Some MB extrinsic neurons extend processes to only a specific layer within a subdomain, defining elemental subdivisions in the lobes, or 'synaptic units' as proposed by Tanaka et al. (2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2008 and is further elaborated upon with new data in this manuscript (Figure 12).

claim: Olfactory perception in the fly is initiated by the binding of an odorant to an ensemble of olfactory sensory neurons in the antennae, resulting in the activation of a distinct and topographically fixed combination of glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: Olfactory perception in the fly is initiated by the binding of an odorant to an ensemble of olfactory sensory neurons in the antennae, resulting in the activation of a distinct and topographically fixed combination of glomeruli in the antennal lobe (Figure 1A,B; reviewed in Vosshall and Stocker (2007); Masse et al. (2009)).
evidence: This is a well-established principle of olfactory system organization, supported by the cited reviews.

claim: Most antennal lobe projection neurons (PNs) extend dendrites to a single glomerulus and project axons that bifurcate to innervate two brain regions, the lateral horn and the MB.
source: Most antennal lobe projection neurons (PNs) extend dendrites to a single glomerulus and project axons that bifurcate to innervate two brain regions, the lateral horn and the MB (Stocker et al., 1990; Wong et al., 2002; Jefferis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The invariant circuitry of the lateral horn is thought to mediate innate behaviors.
source: The invariant circuitry of the lateral horn is thought to mediate innate behaviors, whereas the MB translates olfactory sensory information into learned behavioral responses (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization and functional studies, supported by a citation to Heisenberg et al., 1985.

claim: The MB translates olfactory sensory information into learned behavioral responses.
source: The invariant circuitry of the lateral horn is thought to mediate innate behaviors, whereas the MB translates olfactory sensory information into learned behavioral responses (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heisenberg et al., 1985 and is a central theme of the manuscript.

claim: The PN axons synapse onto the dendrites of the Kenyon cells (KCs) in the MB calyx.
source: The PN axons synapse onto the dendrites of the Kenyon cells (KCs) in the MB calyx; the parallel axons of the KCs form the MB lobes.
evidence: This is a well-established feature of MB anatomy, supported by general knowledge and prior studies.

claim: The parallel axons of the KCs form the MB lobes.
source: The PN axons synapse onto the dendrites of the Kenyon cells (KCs) in the MB calyx; the parallel axons of the KCs form the MB lobes.
evidence: This is a well-established feature of MB anatomy, supported by general knowledge and prior studies.

claim: Odors activate sparse subpopulations of KCs distributed across the MB without spatial preference.
source: Odors activate sparse subpopulations of KCs distributed across the MB without spatial preference (Turner et al., 2008; Honegger et al., 2011; Campbell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior physiological studies.

claim: Each KC receives on average 6.4 inputs from a random combination of glomeruli.
source: Anatomical and physiological studies reveal that each KC receives on average 6.4 inputs from a random combination of glomeruli; that is, knowledge of a single input to a KC provides no information about the identity of the additional inputs, and connections differ in different flies (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Knowledge of a single input to a KC provides no information about the identity of the additional inputs.
source: Anatomical and physiological studies reveal that each KC receives on average 6.4 inputs from a random combination of glomeruli; that is, knowledge of a single input to a KC provides no information about the identity of the additional inputs, and connections differ in different flies (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies demonstrating random connectivity.

claim: KC connections differ in different flies.
source: Anatomical and physiological studies reveal that each KC receives on average 6.4 inputs from a random combination of glomeruli; that is, knowledge of a single input to a KC provides no information about the identity of the additional inputs, and connections differ in different flies (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies demonstrating variability in connectivity across individuals.

claim: The calyx of the MB discards the highly ordered structure of the antennal lobe.
source: Thus, the calyx of the MB discards the highly ordered structure of the antennal lobe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the random connectivity patterns observed between PNs and KCs.

claim: A restoration of order must be imposed downstream to link the KC representation to an appropriate behavioral output.
source: A restoration of order must therefore be imposed downstream to link the KC representation to an appropriate behavioral output.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation that KCs have random connectivity but behavior is organized.

claim: Three classes of KCs extend parallel fibers that form the γ, α′/β′, and α/β lobes of the MB.
source: Three classes of KCs extend parallel fibers that form the γ, α′/β′, and α/β lobes of the MB, where they form synapses with a relatively small number of MB output neurons (MBONs; Figure 1C) (Crittenden et al., 1998; Ito et al., 1998; Strausfeld et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2008; Busch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: KCs form synapses with a relatively small number of MB output neurons (MBONs).
source: Three classes of KCs extend parallel fibers that form the γ, α′/β′, and α/β lobes of the MB, where they form synapses with a relatively small number of MB output neurons (MBONs; Figure 1C) (Crittenden et al., 1998; Ito et al., 1998; Strausfeld et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2007; Tanaka et al., 2008; Busch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies and is a key finding of the current study.

claim: The MBONs have dendrites in the MB lobes and project axons to neuropils outside of the MB.
source: The MBONs have dendrites in the MB lobes and project axons to neuropils outside of the MB.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrated through split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical tracing (Figure 18).

claim: Modulatory input neurons, including dopaminergic neurons (DANs) and octopaminergic neurons, innervate the MB lobes.
source: Modulatory input neurons, including dopaminergic neurons (DANs) and octopaminergic neurons (Nassel and Elekes, 1992; Tanaka et al., 2008; Busch et al., 2009; Mao and Davis, 2009), also innervate the MB lobes.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The MBONs and DANs send their processes to stereotyped locations, defining spatially restricted 'subdomains' in each lobe.
source: The MBONs and DANs send their processes to stereotyped locations, defining spatially restricted 'subdomains' in each lobe (Ito et al., 1998; Tanaka et al., 2008; Mao and Davis, 2009; Pech et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies and is further elaborated upon with new data in this manuscript.

claim: The DANs are the most prevalent modulatory neurons in the MB.
source: The DANs are the most prevalent modulatory neurons in the MB and dopamine is thought to act locally to modify KC–MBON synapses (Aso et al., 2010; Waddell, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, supported by cell counting and anatomical analysis.

claim: Dopamine is thought to act locally to modify KC–MBON synapses.
source: The DANs are the most prevalent modulatory neurons in the MB and dopamine is thought to act locally to modify KC–MBON synapses (Aso et al., 2010; Waddell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and is a prevailing model in the field.

claim: DAN activity is required during learning.
source: In accord with this model, DAN activity is required during learning (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Aso et al., 2010, 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) and exogenous activation of DAN subpopulations can serve as an US in associative learning paradigms (Schroll et al., 2006; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010, 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Exogenous activation of DAN subpopulations can serve as an US in associative learning paradigms.
source: In accord with this model, DAN activity is required during learning (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Aso et al., 2010, 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) and exogenous activation of DAN subpopulations can serve as an US in associative learning paradigms (Schroll et al., 2006; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010, 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior functional studies.

claim: D1-like dopamine receptors in the KCs are necessary to form olfactory memories.
source: In addition, D1-like dopamine receptors in the KCs are necessary to form olfactory memories (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2007.

claim: Different populations of DANs are activated by USs of different valence.
source: Different populations of DANs are activated by USs of different valence; see Figure 1A of the accompanying paper (Aso et al., 2014) for summary (Riemensperger et al., 2005; Mao and Davis, 2009; Liu et al., 2012; Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Genetic manipulation has implicated specific subsets of MBONs in the mediation of learned appetitive and aversive behaviors.
source: Genetic manipulation has also implicated specific subsets of MBONs in the mediation of learned appetitive and aversive behaviors (Sejourne et al., 2011; Pai et al., 2013; Placais et al., 2013; Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior functional studies.

claim: The DANs are the source of the learning cue.
source: These experiments implicate the DANs as the source of the learning cue and the MBONs as the mediators of behavioral output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited functional studies and the anatomical organization described in the manuscript.

claim: The MBONs are the mediators of behavioral output.
source: These experiments implicate the DANs as the source of the learning cue and the MBONs as the mediators of behavioral output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited functional studies and the anatomical organization described in the manuscript.

claim: The MB lobes are composed of ∼2200 neurons that include 7 KC, 21 MBON, and 20 DAN cell types.
source: We found that the MB lobes are composed of ∼2200 neurons that include 7 KC, 21 MBON, and 20 DAN cell types.
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines, cell counting, and anatomical analysis.

claim: The MBONs of a given type exhibit spatially stereotyped dendritic arbors in the MB lobes that form 15 compartments that collectively tile the lobes.
source: The MBONs of a given type exhibit spatially stereotyped dendritic arbors in the MB lobes that form 15 compartments that collectively tile the lobes.
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment and two-color labeling experiments (Figure 10).

claim: Each DAN cell type projects axons to one or at most two of the compartments defined by the MBONs.
source: Each DAN cell type projects axons to one or at most two of the compartments defined by the MBONs.
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, demonstrated through split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical analysis (Figure 12).

claim: The alignment of DAN axons with compartmentalized KC–MBON synapses creates an isolated unit for learning that can transform the disordered KC representation into ordered MBON output.
source: The alignment of DAN axons with compartmentalized KC–MBON synapses creates an isolated unit for learning that can transform the disordered KC representation into ordered MBON output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and prior functional studies.

claim: The MBON axons project to five discrete neuropils outside of the MB, providing loci for the convergence of all the information necessary for learned associative responses.
source: The MBON axons project to five discrete neuropils outside of the MB, providing loci for the convergence of all the information necessary for learned associative responses.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 18).

claim: We screened adult brains from 7000 GAL4 lines driven by known enhancers to identify lines containing neurons that innervate the MB lobes.
source: We screened adult brains from 7000 GAL4 lines driven by known enhancers (Pfeiffer et al., 2008; Jenett et al., 2012) to identify lines containing neurons that innervate the MB lobes.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: We used the split-GAL4 strategy to identify lines with more restricted expression in the MB.
source: We therefore identified lines with overlapping expression patterns for the MB neurons and used the split-GAL4 strategy (Luan et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010) to identify lines with more restricted expression in the MB (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: After screening 2500 such intersections, we obtained more than 400 split-GAL4 combinations that had strong expression in the MB neurons.
source: After screening 2500 such intersections, we obtained more than 400 split-GAL4 combinations that had strong expression in the MB neurons.
evidence: This describes the results of the screening methodology used in the current study.

claim: Most split-GAL4 lines that drive expression in MBONs or DANs contain a small number of neurons that share virtually identical morphologies and exhibit bilateral symmetry.
source: Most split-GAL4 lines that drive expression in MBONs or DANs contain a small number of neurons that share virtually identical morphologies and exhibit bilateral symmetry, and this profile is maintained across different individuals (Figure 2—figure supplements 3–6 and data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on analysis of split-GAL4 driver lines.

claim: The split-GAL4 lines that label the KC contain far greater cell numbers (75–600).
source: The split-GAL4 lines that label the KC contain far greater cell numbers (75–600) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on cell counting in split-GAL4 driver lines.

claim: We operationally define a cell type as a single neuron (per hemisphere) or a group of neurons that is not further subdivided in any of the 7000 GAL4 lines.
source: We operationally define a cell type as a single neuron (per hemisphere) or a group of neurons that is not further subdivided in any of the 7000 GAL4 lines.
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the current study.

claim: Neurons within most cell types exhibit indistinguishable morphology.
source: Moreover, neurons within most cell types exhibit indistinguishable morphology.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on single-cell analysis using multicolor flp-out.

claim: We identified on average 12 GAL4 drivers that label the same cell type within the set of 7000 lines, indicating that the screen was near saturation.
source: Importantly, we identified on average 12 GAL4 drivers that label the same cell type within the set of 7000 lines, indicating that the screen was near saturation in our large GAL4 collection.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, providing evidence for the completeness of the screen.

claim: Photoactivation of the MB labels all neurons that express PA-GFP and project to the MB.
source: Photoactivation of the MB labels all neurons that express PA-GFP and project to the MB (Figure 4A; for limitations, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: Photoactivation of the MB lobes in flies expressing PA-GFP pan-neuronally (except in the KCs) resulted in labeling of eight individual neurons and five clusters of neuronal cell bodies.
source: Photoactivation of the MB lobes in flies expressing PA-GFP pan-neuronally (except in the KCs) resulted in labeling of eight individual neurons and five clusters of neuronal cell bodies (Figure 4, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on photoactivation experiments.

claim: The number and position of PA-GFP labeled neurons matched well with the cells identified in the split-GAL4 lines.
source: The number and position of these PA-GFP labeled neurons matched well with the cells identified in the split-GAL4 lines.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, providing validation of the split-GAL4 approach.

claim: Photoactivation of individual subdomains confirmed the results obtained from the genetic approach.
source: Photoactivation of individual subdomains confirmed the results obtained from the genetic approach (Figure 5), but the photoactivation experiments also revealed two MBONs not identified in the split-GAL4 lines.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, providing validation and extension of the split-GAL4 approach.

claim: Photoactivation experiments revealed two MBONs not identified in the split-GAL4 lines.
source: Photoactivation of individual subdomains confirmed the results obtained from the genetic approach (Figure 5), but the photoactivation experiments also revealed two MBONs not identified in the split-GAL4 lines.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrating the complementary nature of the two approaches.

claim: These two MBONs not identified in the split-GAL4 lines were subsequently identified in the VT-GAL4 collection.
source: These MBONs were subsequently identified in the VT-GAL4 collection, allowing us to characterize their projections (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrating the completeness of the characterization.

claim: The split-GAL4 screen and PA-GFP tracing identified perhaps all of the neurons in the MB lobes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that each cell type defined by our criteria likely represents an irreducible group of equivalent cells, and that the split-GAL4 screen and PA-GFP tracing identified perhaps all of the neurons in the MB lobes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the convergence of results from the split-GAL4 screen and PA-GFP tracing experiments.

claim: We selected 92 split-GAL4 lines representing the best examples for single cell types as well as combinations of related cell types.
source: We selected 92 split-GAL4 lines representing the best examples for single cell types as well as combinations of related cell types; these split-GAL4 lines will facilitate further anatomical and functional characterization of the MB cell types (see Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6, Supplementary file 1, www.janelia.org/split-gal4, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the selection of reagents generated in the current study.

claim: The split-GAL4 approach identified 20 DAN types of the PPL1 and PAM clusters that innervate the MB.
source: The split-GAL4 approach identified 20 DAN types of the PPL1 and PAM clusters that innervate the MB.
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical analysis.

claim: We identified about 30% less DANs in the PAM cluster in our collection of split-GAL4 lines compared to the number estimated by PA-GFP and anti-dopamine immunoreactivity.
source: We identified about 30% less DANs in the PAM cluster in our collection of split-GAL4 lines compared to the number estimated by PA-GFP and anti-dopamine immunoreactivity (Figure 5) (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, comparing results from different methods.

claim: The additional DANs not captured by split-GAL4 lines exhibit innervation patterns similar to those of the split-GAL4 lines.
source: However, these additional DANs exhibit innervation patterns similar to those of the split-GAL4 lines (see below), and therefore we assume that they either represent closely related cell types or that some of our split-GAL4 drivers are stochastic in their expression and fail to label all members of a cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical observations in the current study.

claim: The MB lobes consist of three groups of compartments based on the putative transmitter of MBONs (glutamate, GABA, and acetylcholine).
source: MB lobes consist of three groups of compartments based on the putative transmitter of MBONs (glutamate, GABA, and acetylcholine, shown color-coded).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on immunostaining for neurotransmitter markers (Figure 9).

claim: The five KC types that receive olfactory information are each represented by hundreds of neurons per hemisphere and have their dendrites in the main calyx.
source: The five KC types (γmain, α′/β′ap, α′/β′m, α/βc, and α/βs) that receive olfactory information are each represented by hundreds of neurons per hemisphere and have their dendrites in the main calyx.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting.

claim: Each KC cell type sends axonal projections to a spatially segregated layer in the lobes.
source: Each KC cell type sends axonal projections to a spatially segregated layer in the lobes.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrated through split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical analysis (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: The dendritic arbors of each KC type tend to be found in the same regions of the calyx, but those dendritic zones are largely overlapping.
source: The dendritic arbors of each KC type also tend to be found in the same regions of the calyx (Lin et al., 2007; Leiss et al., 2009), but those dendritic zones are largely overlapping and individual KCs within a given cell type exhibit variable dendritic projection patterns (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis, and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Individual KCs within a given cell type exhibit variable dendritic projection patterns.
source: The dendritic arbors of each KC type also tend to be found in the same regions of the calyx (Lin et al., 2007; Leiss et al., 2009), but those dendritic zones are largely overlapping and individual KCs within a given cell type exhibit variable dendritic projection patterns (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on single-cell analysis.

claim: The KCs receive input from an apparently random collection of glomeruli.
source: Moreover, the KCs receive input from an apparently random collection of glomeruli (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Most neuronal cell types in the olfactory pathway of the fly consist of one to ten neurons that exhibit stereotyped projections.
source: These features are in sharp contrast to most neuronal cell types in the olfactory pathway of the fly that are thought to consist of one to ten neurons that exhibit stereotyped projections (Yu et al., 2010), suggesting that their input and output connections are genetically predetermined.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2010 and is general knowledge in the field.

claim: The input and output connections of most neuronal cell types in the olfactory pathway of the fly are genetically predetermined.
source: These features are in sharp contrast to most neuronal cell types in the olfactory pathway of the fly that are thought to consist of one to ten neurons that exhibit stereotyped projections (Yu et al., 2010), suggesting that their input and output connections are genetically predetermined.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stereotyped projections observed in these cell types.

claim: The unique features of the KCs suggest a unique function in the processing of olfactory information.
source: These observations suggest a unique function of the KCs in the processing of olfactory information (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference based on the distinctive features of KCs compared to other olfactory neurons.

claim: We identified 34 MBONs that comprise 21 different cell types.
source: By determining the polarity of each cell type using high-resolution confocal imaging along with an analysis of the expression of the presynaptic reporter synaptotagmin-smGFP-HA (Syt::smGFP-HA; Figure 8), we identified 34 MBONs that comprise 21 different cell types (Table 1, Figure 3B, Video 3).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines, polarity determination, and anatomical analysis.

claim: We employed immunostaining to identify MBON types as either cholinergic, glutamatergic, or GABAergic.
source: We employed immunostaining to identify MBON types as either cholinergic, glutamatergic, or GABAergic (Figure 9, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: MBONs that use the same neurotransmitter extend dendrites to adjacent regions of the lobes.
source: MBONs that use the same neurotransmitter extend dendrites to adjacent regions of the lobes; cholinergic MBONs in the vertical (α and α′) lobes, glutamatergic MBONs in the medial (β, β′, and γ) lobes, and GABAergic MBONs in an area of the lobes at the intersection between these two regions (Figure 9 and Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on immunostaining and anatomical analysis (Figure 9).

claim: Fourteen MBON cell types consist of only one cell per hemisphere.
source: Fourteen MBON cell types consist of only one cell per hemisphere, six types contain two cells, and one type eight cells per hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting.

claim: Six MBON types contain two cells per hemisphere.
source: Fourteen MBON cell types consist of only one cell per hemisphere, six types contain two cells, and one type eight cells per hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting.

claim: One MBON type contains eight cells per hemisphere.
source: Fourteen MBON cell types consist of only one cell per hemisphere, six types contain two cells, and one type eight cells per hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting.

claim: Single cell analysis revealed that each member of an MBON type exhibits indistinguishable morphology as assessed by light microscopy.
source: Single cell analysis revealed that each member of an MBON type exhibits indistinguishable morphology as assessed by light microscopy, and these stereotyped projection patterns are invariant across flies (see below for all cell types).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on multicolor flp-out experiments.

claim: The stereotyped projection patterns of MBONs are invariant across flies.
source: Single cell analysis revealed that each member of an MBON type exhibits indistinguishable morphology as assessed by light microscopy, and these stereotyped projection patterns are invariant across flies (see below for all cell types).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on analysis of multiple individuals.

claim: The 21 MBON types elaborate dendritic arbors in insular, segregated domains of the lobes that we call compartments.
source: The 21 MBON types elaborate dendritic arbors in insular, segregated domains of the lobes that we call compartments.
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment and two-color labeling experiments (Figure 10).

claim: MBON dendritic arbors within each compartment exhibit little, if any, overlap with arbors in neighboring compartments.
source: MBON dendritic arbors within each compartment exhibit little, if any, overlap with arbors in neighboring compartments (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment and two-color labeling experiments (Figure 10, Figure 11).

claim: Computational alignment of the dendritic arbors of each of the MBON types within a single reference brain revealed that these compartments collectively tile the MB lobes with minimal overlap.
source: Computational alignment of the dendritic arbors of each of the MBON types within a single reference brain revealed that these compartments collectively tile the MB lobes with minimal overlap (Figure 10G,I,K).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment (Figure 10).

claim: The alignment reveals gaps between arbors at four compartment borders.
source: The alignment reveals gaps between arbors at four compartment borders; staining of the MB lobes for the presynaptic marker Bruchpilot (Figure 10—figure supplement 1) suggests that these gaps represent areas of reduced synaptic density.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment and immunostaining (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).

claim: Two-color labeling experiments confirmed that the dendritic arbors of different MBONs are segregated in spatially stereotyped compartments.
source: Two-color labeling experiments confirmed that the dendritic arbors of different MBONs are segregated in spatially stereotyped compartments (Figure 11A–C).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, providing validation of the computational alignment results (Figure 11).

claim: We observed ensheathing glia at the borders between the MB lobes but not between the MBON compartments in each lobe.
source: We observed ensheathing glia at the borders between the MB lobes but not between the MBON compartments in each lobe (Figure 11J–L).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on two-color labeling experiments (Figure 11J–L).

claim: 13 of the 21 MBON types extend dendrites to a single compartment.
source: 13 of the 21 MBON types extend dendrites to a single compartment, and 8 MBON types project to two compartments (Figure 12A–C).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis (Figure 12).

claim: 8 MBON types project to two compartments.
source: 13 of the 21 MBON types extend dendrites to a single compartment, and 8 MBON types project to two compartments (Figure 12A–C).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis (Figure 12).

claim: Most of the MBON types innervate KCs from each of the layers within a compartment, but eight types restrict their dendritic arbors to specific layers.
source: Most of the MBON types innervate KCs from each of the layers within a compartment, but eight types restrict their dendritic arbors to specific layers (Figure 11D, 12A,C,D).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis (Figure 11D, Figure 12).

claim: The convergence of 2000 KCs onto just 34 MBONs suggests that the MBONs do not represent odor identity but instead provide a representation that may bias behavioral responses.
source: The identification of the full complement of 21 MBON types highlights the extensive convergence of 2000 KCs onto just 34 MBONs, a number even smaller than the number of glomeruli in the AL. Thus, the high-dimensional KC representation of odor identity is transformed into a low-dimensional MB output. This suggests that the MBONs do not represent odor identity but instead provide a representation that may bias behavioral responses (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study.

claim: Our split-GAL4 screen identified over 100 DANs of 20 types.
source: Our split-GAL4 screen identified over 100 DANs of 20 types (Figure 3C, Table 1 and Video 4).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and anatomical analysis.

claim: Each DAN type contains a small number of neurons: DAN types from the PPL1 cluster contain one or two cells per hemisphere and DAN types from the PAM cluster contain up to ∼20 cells per hemisphere.
source: Each DAN type contains a small number of neurons: DAN types from the PPL1 cluster contain one or two cells per hemisphere and DAN types from the PAM cluster contain up to ∼20 cells per hemisphere (Table 1, see Figures 14–16 for each cell type, see 'Materials and methods' for classification).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting.

claim: The axon terminals of the DANs project to specific compartments and, similar to the dendrites of MBONs, tile the entire MB lobes.
source: The axon terminals of the DANs project to specific compartments and, similar to the dendrites of MBONs, tile the entire MB lobes (Figure 10H,J,L, 14–16 and Video 4).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment (Figure 10).

claim: 17 of the 20 DAN types project to only a single compartment.
source: 17 of the 20 DAN types project to only a single compartment (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis (Figure 12).

claim: Two-color labeling and multicolor flp-out of DANs innervating neighboring compartments show clear segregation of their axon termini.
source: Two-color labeling and multicolor flp-out of DANs innervating neighboring compartments show clear segregation of their axon termini (Figure 11E,F and data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, providing validation of the computational alignment results (Figure 11).

claim: Two-color labeling experiments revealed overlap of the axon termini of DAN types and the dendritic arbors of cognate MBON types that innervate the same compartment.
source: Two-color labeling experiments revealed overlap of the axon termini of DAN types and the dendritic arbors of cognate MBON types that innervate the same compartment (Figure 11G–I).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, demonstrating the spatial alignment of DANs and MBONs (Figure 11).

claim: Computational alignment to a single reference brain demonstrates that the DAN axon termini tile the MB lobes.
source: Computational alignment to a single reference brain extends these observations to all DAN types and further demonstrates that the DAN axon termini tile the MB lobes (Figure 10H,J,L).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, demonstrated through computational alignment (Figure 10).

claim: Different MBON types have access to largely equivalent input from the KCs but are modulated by different DANs.
source: Thus, different MBON types have access to largely equivalent input from the KCs but are modulated by different DANs (Figures 12 and 13).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study (Figures 12 and 13).

claim: In classical learning paradigms, different DAN types respond to different unconditioned stimuli (US).
source: In classical learning paradigms, different DAN types respond to different unconditioned stimuli (US) (Riemensperger et al., 2005; Mao and Davis, 2009; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior functional studies.

claim: The compartmental organization suggests that the DANs may convey information about the US to specific MBON types.
source: The compartmental organization we observe suggests that the DANs may convey information about the US to specific MBON types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and prior functional studies.

claim: Dopamine release in specific compartments may modify local KC–MBON synapses to bias behavioral output.
source: Dopamine release in specific compartments may modify local KC–MBON synapses to bias behavioral output.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and prior functional studies.

claim: We identified three MBONs and one DAN type that appear to interconnect different compartments of the MB lobes.
source: We identified three MBONs and one DAN type that appear to interconnect different compartments of the MB lobes (Figure 12A, Figure 14—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 17A–D).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing (Figure 17).

claim: Each of the three MBONs that interconnect compartments projects to the compartments of other MBONs but not back to the compartment occupied by its own dendrites.
source: Each of these three MBONs projects to the compartments of other MBONs but not back to the compartment occupied by its own dendrites.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing (Figure 17).

claim: Information flows in one direction through the MBON connections, and these MBON connections could create a multi-layered feedforward network.
source: Thus information flows in one direction, and these MBON connections could create a multi-layered feedforward network (Figure 17J, see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study (Figure 17).

claim: 12 of the MBON types receive input from the KCs but not from other MBONs and therefore read out KC activity as a single output layer.
source: 12 of the MBON types receive input from the KCs but not from other MBONs and therefore read out KC activity as a single output layer.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis (Figure 17).

claim: Most of the MBONs having dendrites in the α′/β′ and γ lobes provide a single-layer readout.
source: Most of the MBONs having dendrites in the α′/β′ and γ lobes provide such a single-layer readout.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical analysis (Figure 17).

claim: The glutamatergic MBON whose dendrites arborize in the γ4 compartment projects axons into the γ1 and γ2 compartments as well as to neuropils outside the MB.
source: In contrast, the glutamatergic MBON whose dendrites arborize in the γ4 compartment projects axons into the γ1 and γ2 compartments as well as to neuropils outside the MB (Figure 17A,G–I).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing (Figure 17).

claim: The γ1 and γ2 MBONs have access to direct KC input as well as to the input provided by the γ4 MBON.
source: Thus, the γ1 and γ2 MBONs have access to direct KC input as well as to the input provided by the γ4 MBON.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study (Figure 17).

claim: The outputs of the γ1 and γ2 MBONs reflect a two-layer feedforward network.
source: The outputs of these two γ lobe compartments thus reflect a two-layer feedforward network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study (Figure 17).

claim: The readout of the α/β lobe is more elaborate because the γ1 MBON projects to all of the compartments of the α/β lobe.
source: The readout of the α/β lobe is even more elaborate because the γ1 MBON projects to all of the compartments of the α/β lobe (Figure 17C,E,F), and the β1 MBON projects to the α1, α2, and α3 compartments (Figure 17B).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing (Figure 17).

claim: The β1 MBON projects to the α1, α2, and α3 compartments.
source: The readout of the α/β lobe is even more elaborate because the γ1 MBON projects to all of the compartments of the α/β lobe (Figure 17C,E,F), and the β1 MBON projects to the α1, α2, and α3 compartments (Figure 17B).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing (Figure 17).

claim: The α1, α2, and α3 MBONs represent a four-layer feedforward network with access to the KC activity of the α/β and γ lobes, both directly and indirectly through MBON intermediaries.
source: The α1, α2, and α3 MBONs thus represent a four-layer feedforward network with access to the KC activity of the α/β and γ lobes, both directly and indirectly through MBON intermediaries (Figure 17J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study (Figure 17).

claim: The DAN cell type that projects axons to the γ4 compartment extends dendrites to the γ1 and γ2 compartments.
source: The DAN cell type that projects axons to the γ4 compartment (Figure 17D) provides another form of communication between compartments. This cell type extends dendrites to the γ1 and γ2 compartments, where they appear to receive direct inputs from the axonal termini of MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 (Figure 17G–I), creating a recurrent loop involving modulatory dopamine input.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing (Figure 17).

claim: The dendrites of the DAN cell type that projects to γ4 appear to receive direct inputs from the axonal termini of MBON-γ4>γ1γ2, creating a recurrent loop involving modulatory dopamine input.
source: The DAN cell type that projects axons to the γ4 compartment (Figure 17D) provides another form of communication between compartments. This cell type extends dendrites to the γ1 and γ2 compartments, where they appear to receive direct inputs from the axonal termini of MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 (Figure 17G–I), creating a recurrent loop involving modulatory dopamine input.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on anatomical tracing and two-color labeling experiments (Figure 17).

claim: The MBON axons that innervate other compartments within the MB lobes have access to dopamine inputs and thus can potentially be modified by learning.
source: The MBON axons that innervate other compartments within the MB lobes have access to dopamine inputs and thus can potentially be modified by learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study.

claim: Adaptive multi-layer or 'deep' feedforward networks are capable of more complex readout functions than single-layer readouts.
source: Adaptive multi-layer or 'deep' feedforward networks are known to be capable of more complex readout functions than single-layer readouts (Bishop, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bishop, 2006, a standard reference in machine learning.

claim: The four-layer α lobe readout system may support more sophisticated neuronal computations than the one- and two-layer γ or α′/β′ lobe systems.
source: Thus, the four-layer α lobe readout system may support more sophisticated neuronal computations than the one- and two-layer γ or α′/β′ lobe systems.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and principles from machine learning.

claim: The 34 MBONs represent the sole outputs of the MB lobes.
source: The 34 MBONs represent the sole outputs of the MB lobes.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on the comprehensive screen and PA-GFP tracing experiments.

claim: Computational alignment of single-cell images allowed us to localize the axon termini of the MBONs outside the MB.
source: Computational alignment of single-cell images allowed us to localize the axon termini of the MBONs outside the MB.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: The axon terminals of the MBONs converge onto five neuropils: the crepine (CRE), the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP), the superior intermediate protocerebrum (SIP), the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), and the lateral horn (LH).
source: The axon terminals of the MBONs (Figure 18) converge onto five neuropils: the crepine (CRE; a region surrounding the horizontal/medial lobes), the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP), the superior intermediate protocerebrum (SIP), the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), and the lateral horn (LH) (Figure 18E).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 18).

claim: Most MBON types project axons to several of the five neuropils.
source: Most MBON types project axons to several of these neuropils (Figure 18—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 18—figure supplement 1).

claim: Within a neuropil, the axon terminals of each MBON type exhibit distinct and confined projection patterns, suggesting that different MBON types may synapse onto different neurons.
source: Within a neuropil, the axon terminals of each MBON type exhibit distinct and confined projection patterns, suggesting that different MBON types may synapse onto different neurons (Figure 19, also see Figures 14–16 for individual MBON projection patterns).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 19).

claim: We observed significant overlap between the axon terminals of different MBONs, suggesting that in certain cases MBONs may converge onto the same post-synaptic target neuron.
source: However, we also observed significant overlap between the axon terminals of different MBONs, suggesting that in certain cases MBONs may converge onto the same post-synaptic target neuron (Figure 20A,D,E).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 20).

claim: Two-color labeling experiments confirmed the overlap of MBON axon terminals for a subset of MBONs.
source: These results, obtained by computational alignment, were confirmed for a subset of MBONs by two-color labeling experiments (Figure 20J–L; Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, providing validation of the computational alignment results (Figure 20).

claim: Computational alignment of single cell images of each DAN type identified the dendritic arbors of the DANs outside the MB.
source: Computational alignment of single cell images of each DAN type identified the dendritic arbors of the DANs outside the MB (Figure 18D).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: 90% of the dendritic arbors of the DANs reside in four of the neuropils targeted by the MBONs: CRE, SMP, SIP, and SLP.
source: Interestingly, 90% of the dendritic arbors of the DANs reside in four of the neuropils targeted by the MBONs: CRE, SMP, SIP, and SLP (Figures 18E and 19).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of DAN dendrites (Figure 18).

claim: Because DANs are activated by unconditioned stimuli (US), the neuropils CRE, SMP, SIP, and SLP are likely targets of the US input.
source: Because DANs are activated by unconditioned stimuli (US), these neuropils are likely targets of the US input (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and prior functional studies.

claim: We observed cases where the dendrites of different DAN types in a single neuropil overlap, suggesting that they may share upstream input.
source: We observed cases where the dendrites of different DAN types in a single neuropil overlap (Figure 20B,F,G), suggesting that they may share upstream input.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of DAN dendrites (Figure 20).

claim: We observed overlap between MBON terminals and DAN dendrites within each neuropil, implying that some MBONs may synapse on specific DANs.
source: Furthermore, we observed overlap between MBON terminals and DAN dendrites within each neuropil, implying that some MBONs may synapse on specific DANs (Figure 20C,H,I).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment (Figure 20).

claim: In some cases, the axon terminals of an MBON overlap with the dendrites of the DAN type innervating the same compartment, which may provide feedback that regulates dopamine release and hence learning.
source: In some cases, the axon terminals of an MBON overlap with the dendrites of the DAN type innervating the same compartment (Figure 20H). This may provide feedback that regulates dopamine release and hence learning.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment (Figure 20), and the inference about feedback is speculative.

claim: In other cases, axon termini of MBONs from one compartment overlap with the dendrites of DAN types projecting to different compartments, providing a pathway through which the activity of one MBON could modulate the synapses between KCs and MBONs of other compartments.
source: In other cases, axon termini of MBONs from one compartment overlap with the dendrites of DAN types projecting to different compartments (Figure 20I). This provides a pathway through which the activity of one MBON could modulate the synapses between KCs and MBONs of other compartments.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment (Figure 20), and the inference about modulation is speculative.

claim: The MBONs are thought to elicit learned behavioral responses.
source: The MBONs are thought to elicit learned behavioral responses, and it is therefore of interest that four MBON types project to the lateral horn (Figure 18—figure supplement 1), a brain region responsible for innate odor responses (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by prior functional studies and is a prevailing model in the field.

claim: Four MBON types project to the lateral horn.
source: The MBONs are thought to elicit learned behavioral responses, and it is therefore of interest that four MBON types project to the lateral horn (Figure 18—figure supplement 1), a brain region responsible for innate odor responses (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 18—figure supplement 1).

claim: The lateral horn is a brain region responsible for innate odor responses.
source: The MBONs are thought to elicit learned behavioral responses, and it is therefore of interest that four MBON types project to the lateral horn (Figure 18—figure supplement 1), a brain region responsible for innate odor responses (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heisenberg et al., 1985 and is general knowledge in the field.

claim: These cholinergic MBONs may exploit LH neurons capable of eliciting innate behaviors to generate learned olfactory responses.
source: These cholinergic MBONs may exploit LH neurons capable of eliciting innate behaviors to generate learned olfactory responses (Sejourne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and a citation to Sejourne et al., 2011.

claim: The connection between MBONs and the lateral horn may serve to modulate innate behavioral responses as a consequence of learning.
source: This connection may also serve to modulate innate behavioral responses as a consequence of learning.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study.

claim: Most of the MBON outputs do not target the LH but converge onto the neuropils surrounding the MB.
source: Most of the MBON outputs, however, do not target the LH but converge onto the neuropils surrounding the MB (Figure 18).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, based on computational alignment of MBON axon terminals (Figure 18).

claim: The convergent loci of MBON outputs also receive projections from the antennal lobe and the lateral horn and are likely to be major sites of integration and processing of information within the fly brain.
source: These convergent loci also receive projections from the antennal lobe and the lateral horn and are likely to be major sites of integration and processing of information within the fly brain (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical organization observed in the current study and the accompanying paper.

claim: Most of the cell types in the olfactory circuit comprise small groups containing from one to 20 neurons.
source: Most of the cell types in the olfactory circuit—the MBONs and the DANs as well as the olfactory sensory neurons, the PNs, and the LH neurons (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Masse et al., 2009)—comprise small groups containing from one to 20 neurons (Tanaka et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2008, 2012; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies and is general knowledge in the field.

claim: Neurons within most cell types in the olfactory circuit share highly stereotyped projection patterns that superimpose across different individuals.
source: Furthermore, neurons within these groups share highly stereotyped projection patterns that superimpose across different individuals (this work) (Marin et al., 2002; Datta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and is a finding of the current study.

claim: The stereotyped projection patterns of most olfactory circuit neurons suggest that the input and output connections of these neurons are genetically determined.
source: This suggests that the input and output connections of these neurons are genetically determined (Ruta et al., 2010; Kohl et al., 2013; Fisek and Wilson, 2014), although these may be subject to plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stereotyped projections observed, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The connections of most olfactory circuit neurons may be subject to plasticity.
source: This suggests that the input and output connections of these neurons are genetically determined (Ruta et al., 2010; Kohl et al., 2013; Fisek and Wilson, 2014), although these may be subject to plasticity.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging the possibility of plasticity despite stereotyped projections.

claim: The KCs of the MB comprise 2000 neurons that define only seven distinct cell types.
source: In contrast, the KCs of the MB comprise 2000 neurons that define only seven distinct cell types, receive unstructured, rather than stereotyped, inputs (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013), and connect to multiple MBONs through plastic synapses (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007, 2012).
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study, based on split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting.

claim: KCs receive unstructured, rather than stereotyped, inputs.
source: In contrast, the KCs of the MB comprise 2000 neurons that define only seven distinct cell types, receive unstructured, rather than stereotyped, inputs (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013), and connect to multiple MBONs through plastic synapses (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: KCs connect to multiple MBONs through plastic synapses.
source: In contrast, the KCs of the MB comprise 2000 neurons that define only seven distinct cell types, receive unstructured, rather than stereotyped, inputs (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013), and connect to multiple MBONs through plastic synapses (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007, 2012.

claim: The distinctive features of the KCs afford the MB the ability to contextualize novel sensory experiences, consistent with its role in mediating learned olfactory associations and behavior.
source: These distinctive features of the KCs afford the MB the ability to contextualize novel sensory experiences, consistent with its role in mediating learned olfactory associations and behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distinctive features of KCs and the known role of the MB in learning.

claim: In the representation of odors by the antennal lobe projection neurons, every odor can be thought of as a point in an approximately 50 dimensional space, each dimension corresponding to a particular glomerulus.
